subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
passage:
Nanny's notebook, Saturday
Charu's red toy car stopped going vroom mid-race. She shook it once, listened, then walked it straight to her father, Pankaj, who was on the balcony. She held it up at his face and said firmly, "No." He took it, found the loose battery lid, pressed it shut, and the car roared. Charu grabbed it and ran. It seems she expects Papa to fix everything.

qa.q: Where was Pankaj when Charu brought the car?
qa.a: He was on the balcony.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she held the car up and said "No"?
qa.a: She was annoyed that the car had gone quiet and confident that Papa would fix it.

qa.q: What else could Pankaj try so Charu learns a little too?
qa.a: He could show her the loose lid and let her press it shut, so next time she has one step to try herself.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see being handed the car?
qa.a: He probably finds it sweet and funny to be treated as the repair shop, and fixes it quickly.

grounding: A caregiver's note records a toddler carrying a silent toy car to her father and saying "no," treating him as the repair service.

subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
passage: On the mud floor of their house in a Jharkhand village, Nikita's tin car went silent. She looked at it, then toddled across to Baba, who was sharpening a sickle by the door. She pushed the car into his lap. "No!" she said, and pointed at it. Baba set the sickle far aside, turned the car over and wound the key. It whirred again. Her sister Arohi cheered.

qa.q: What was Baba sharpening?
qa.a: He was sharpening a sickle.

qa.q: What does Nikita's firm "No!" suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was upset and cross that the car had stopped, and sure Baba could fix it.

qa.q: What would you advise Baba to show Nikita next?
qa.a: He could show her the key and let her try turning it, so she learns part of the fix herself.

qa.q: How does Arohi see the car being fixed?
qa.a: Arohi is happy and excited for her sister, cheering when the car whirs again.

grounding: A toddler carries her silent toy car to her father and says "no," treating him as the one who repairs things.

passage:
Written by Nilesh's Dadi, Tuesday
Whenever something breaks, my daughter-in-law Ritu calls "Dadi!" and I come. Today Nilesh's sandal strap slipped off its buckle. He looked at it, looked at the door to my room and shouted, "Dadi! Dadi!" Just the way Ritu does. I came, fixed the strap and laughed. He watched my hands the whole time.

qa.q: What slipped off its buckle?
qa.a: Nilesh's sandal strap slipped off its buckle.

qa.q: What was Nilesh thinking when he shouted "Dadi!"?
qa.a: He seemed sure and hopeful that calling Dadi, the way Ritu does, would fix the broken strap.

qa.q: What else could Dadi try so Nilesh learns more than calling?
qa.a: She could fix the strap slowly while he watches, and next time let him try pushing it through the buckle.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel hearing that Nilesh copies her?
qa.a: Ritu would probably feel amused and a little surprised to learn he copies her call so exactly.

grounding: A grandmother's note describes a toddler who copies his mother's habit of calling "Dadi!" when something breaks.

passage: The house near the canal in Bhatinda had three rooms, and Dadi was usually in the far one. When a pot handle came loose, Shalini called, "Dadi!" When the tap dripped, "Dadi!" Jaya, her toddler, was watching. On Sunday Jaya's shoe strap came undone. She looked down, then turned toward the far room and yelled, "Dadiii!" Dadi came in, hands floury, and fixed it.

qa.q: Where was Dadi usually?
qa.a: She was usually in the far room.

qa.q: What was Jaya thinking when she yelled toward the far room?
qa.a: She seemed confident that yelling "Dadi", like Shalini does, is how broken things get fixed.

qa.q: What else could Shalini show Jaya?
qa.a: She could show her how to fasten the strap herself, so Jaya learns another way besides calling.

qa.q: How does Dadi see Jaya's call?
qa.a: Dadi probably finds it funny and endearing, since she comes at once even with floury hands.

grounding: A toddler copies her mother calling "Dadi!" when things break and shouts it when her own shoe strap comes loose.

passage: In the small Prague flat, Bao's toy drum stopped beeping. He shook it hard. Nothing. He banged it on the floorboards, once, twice. Silence. He pressed the round button, press, press, press, press, looking closer each time. Still nothing. Then he stood up, tucked the drum under one arm and set off down the hallway calling, "Mama? Mama!" Olga put her head out of the bathroom.

qa.q: What did Bao do right after the drum stopped beeping?
qa.a: He shook it hard.

qa.q: What was Bao feeling as he pressed the button again and again?
qa.a: He was puzzled and frustrated, looking closer each time because it still did nothing.

qa.q: Which approach worked in the end, and why?
qa.a: Going to find Mama after trying alone, because she may know about batteries or switches he can't fix.

qa.q: How might Olga feel seeing Bao come down the hallway?
qa.a: She would probably feel curious and ready to help, since he tried first and then came to her.

grounding: A toddler tries shaking, banging and pressing a silent toy, then sets off to find his mother when none of it works.

passage: I'm Vasudha from the flat upstairs, and I was waiting for Yash's mother to return my tiffin. Yash was on the floor with his toy phone. It had stopped singing. He shook it. He banged it on the tiles. He pressed the green button, again and again. Then he stood, the phone clutched to his chest, and went looking room by room until he found his mother. I don't know what he felt, but he didn't cry once.

qa.q: What had stopped singing?
qa.a: Yash's toy phone had stopped singing.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling as she watched Yash?
qa.a: Vasudha was impressed and a little surprised that Yash tried so many things and didn't cry once.

qa.q: What would you advise Yash's mother to do when he finds her?
qa.a: She could show him what is wrong with the phone, so his own tries next time include that step.

qa.q: How might it feel for Yash when his mother takes the phone?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and hopeful, after trying everything alone first.

grounding: An observer watches a toddler shake, bang and press a silent toy before going to find his mother.

passage: Thomas's teddy slid behind the sofa in the house on the church lane in Pala. He poked his arm into the gap; it wouldn't reach. So he stood where he was and screamed, again and again, not moving. In the kitchen, Rajni heard it and thought he had fallen. She checked his knees, his hands, his head. Only after five minutes did she see his finger pointing at the gap.

qa.q: Where did the teddy slide?
qa.a: It slid behind the sofa.

qa.q: What was Rajni thinking when she heard the screaming?
qa.a: She was worried and alarmed, thinking he had fallen, so she checked him all over.

qa.q: What else could Thomas do next time to get help faster?
qa.a: He could walk to Rajni and pull her to the sofa or point right away, so she knows the problem is the teddy.

qa.q: How does the screaming feel from Rajni's side?
qa.a: It is frightening and confusing for her, because the noise tells her something is wrong but not what.

grounding: A toddler screams from the spot when his teddy is wedged behind the sofa, and his caregiver cannot tell what is wrong, so help is slow.

passage: Anders stood by the sofa in the Malmö flat and howled. His bear had dropped behind the cushions, into the dark crack at the back. He did not move toward anyone. He just howled. Vera ran in from the hallway, holding one boot. "Are you hurt? Anders, where does it hurt?" He howled louder. It took her a long time to notice the bear's ear poking up.

qa.q: What was Vera holding when she ran in?
qa.a: She was holding one boot.

qa.q: What was Anders feeling as he howled louder?
qa.a: He was frustrated and upset that Vera didn't understand, and that his bear was stuck.

qa.q: What would you change first to help Anders?
qa.a: Teach him to point or lead Vera to the problem, because howling on the spot tells her something is wrong but not what.

qa.q: What is it like for Vera to hear the howl?
qa.a: It is alarming for Vera: she thinks he is hurt and searches for an injury while the real problem waits.

grounding: A toddler howls from where he stands when his bear is stuck behind the sofa, and his mother cannot tell what is wrong.

subtype: Approach: leading the caregiver by hand [Revision]
passage: My name is Gopika, and I was visiting Omkar's mother on Saturday. His ball had rolled under the sofa. "Aai, ball!" he said. She was chopping and said, "Wait a minute." Omkar stood still for a second. Then he grabbed her finger and pulled, hard, all the way to the sofa, and pointed under it. She laughed and knelt. I thought, he's worked out that talking wasn't enough.

qa.q: What did Omkar's mother say when he first asked?
qa.a: She said, "Wait a minute."

qa.q: What was Gopika thinking as she watched Omkar pull his mother?
qa.a: Gopika felt impressed and amused, sensing Omkar had worked out that talking wasn't enough.

qa.q: What else could Omkar's mother do next time?
qa.a: She could look where he points straight away, so he doesn't need to drag her.

qa.q: What might being led by the finger be like for Omkar's mother?
qa.a: She is pulled away from chopping but sees the problem instantly, which makes her laugh.

grounding: An observer watches a toddler pull his mother by the finger to the sofa after she says "wait a minute," bringing her to the problem.

subtype: Approach: leading the caregiver by hand [Revision]
passage:
Monday: Baljeet's teddy went under the divan. "Mama!" he called. Kalyani said, "Wait a minute," and forgot.
Wednesday: the teddy went under again. "Mama!" "Wait a minute." Baljeet waited, then trotted over, gripped her finger and tugged her to the divan, pointing.
Friday: before calling at all, Baljeet took her finger and led her there.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do on Friday?
qa.a: Before calling at all, he took her finger and led her there.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when Kalyani forgot on Monday?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and frustrated that his teddy stayed under the divan.

qa.q: What would you change first if you were Kalyani?
qa.a: Come and look when he first calls, so he knows asking works and needn't tug.

qa.q: How does Baljeet's new plan look to Kalyani?
qa.a: She finds she can't miss the message any more, which may make her realise how often she said wait.

grounding: Over several days a toddler learns to lead his mother by the finger to the problem after "wait a minute" leaves him unheard.

passage: Pallavi's cloth teddy slipped behind the heavy cot in the house near the temple tank. She reached into the gap. Stuck. She reached again, then stood, turned and wandered out to the courtyard to play with the goat's kid. She didn't tell anyone. Two days later, sweeping, her grandfather Gautam found the dusty teddy and held it up. "Pallavi! Look who was hiding!"

qa.q: Who found the teddy?
qa.a: Her grandfather Gautam found it.

qa.q: What might Pallavi have been feeling when she wandered out?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated and gave up, turning to the goat's kid to forget the stuck teddy.

qa.q: What else could Pallavi try next time?
qa.a: She could take Gautam's hand and lead him to the cot, so the teddy comes back the same day.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel finding the teddy?
qa.a: He is happy and playful about it, holding it up and calling her.

grounding: A toddler gives up on a wedged teddy, walks away without telling anyone, and the toy stays lost until her grandfather finds it.

passage: Diego pushed his fist behind the sofa in the Valencia flat, but the stuffed dog was wedged too far. He pulled his arm back, looked at the gap, and toddled off to the balcony to watch pigeons. He said nothing to anyone. That night he cried at bedtime without the dog. The next morning his father Gabriel moved the sofa and found it. "There you are!"

qa.q: Where was Diego's stuffed dog?
qa.a: It was wedged behind the sofa.

qa.q: What was Diego feeling at bedtime?
qa.a: He was sad and upset without his dog, crying at bedtime.

qa.q: What would you advise Diego to try when a toy gets stuck?
qa.a: Go and get Gabriel and point at the gap, so it can be found before bedtime.

qa.q: How might Gabriel see the lost dog?
qa.a: Gabriel probably feels relieved when he finds it, and may wish Diego had told him the day before.

grounding: A toddler stops trying when his toy is wedged, tells no one, and it stays lost until his father finds it later.

subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
passage:
Monday: Farhan finished his khichdi and banged the empty katori on the floor. Mehak asked, "What?" He shouted, "Aur!" She didn't catch it.
Wednesday: he carried the empty katori to Mehak and tapped it twice with a finger. "Aur." She laughed. "More? Okay."
Friday: after the first helping he walked over again, held the katori up and tapped it before saying anything.

qa.q: What did Farhan eat on Monday?
qa.a: He finished his khichdi.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when Mehak didn't understand on Monday?
qa.a: He was frustrated and impatient, shouting because he was still hungry.

qa.q: What worked better, and why?
qa.a: Bringing the katori and tapping it, because the empty bowl in Mehak's hands says "more" clearly even if the word is unclear.

qa.q: How does the katori plan look to Mehak?
qa.a: She finds it easy to understand and funny, laughing and serving him more.

grounding: Over several days a toddler learns to carry an empty katori to his mother and tap it, which says "more" better than the word alone.

subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
passage: The fan whirred in the Ahmedabad flat as Farida wiped the counter. A small tap-tap came from her knee. Hansa stood there holding up her empty katori, tapping the steel side with one finger. "Aur," she said. Then, in case Farida missed it, she pressed the bowl against her mother's hand. Farida smiled, filled it with dal and rice, and Hansa carried it back to her mat.

qa.q: What did Farida fill the katori with?
qa.a: She filled it with dal and rice.

qa.q: What was Hansa wanting when she pressed the bowl into her mother's hand?
qa.a: She was eager and hungry for more, and wanted to be sure Farida understood.

qa.q: What else could Farida do to build on Hansa's plan?
qa.a: She could say "more" while filling it, giving Hansa the word to go with the gesture.

qa.q: How does the tap on her knee feel to Farida?
qa.a: It is a clear and gentle message, easy to answer while she works.

grounding: A toddler brings her empty katori to her mother and taps it, saying "aur," so the bowl carries the message.

passage:
"Jaggu, what are you doing?" Rukmini called.
Jagdish was pulling at the low cupboard handle. "Bikki!"
"Biscuits are locked, kanna."
He let go, trotted to the fridge and heaved at the handle. It didn't move. "Bikki!"
"That's the fridge."
He turned and pointed up at the counter, at the fruit basket. "Nana!"
"Banana? That one I can do."

qa.q: What did Jagdish point at on the counter?
qa.a: He pointed up at the fruit basket.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he moved from cupboard to fridge?
qa.a: He was hungry and determined, not giving up when each handle didn't open.

qa.q: What else could Rukmini do to help Jagdish?
qa.a: She could keep a small snack he can reach, so his search ends sooner and he learns where food is.

qa.q: How does Jagdish's search look to Rukmini?
qa.a: She sees him testing each place in turn and finds it funny, and is happy to give a banana.

grounding: A toddler tugs at a cupboard, then the fridge, then points at the counter, each try showing what he can and cannot reach.

passage:
Home note, Thursday, from Ganga
Vikas was hungry at four. He went to the biscuit cupboard first and pulled; it has a child lock. He went to the fridge and pulled the handle with both hands; too heavy. Then he stood by the counter, pointed up at the steel box of murmura and looked at me. I gave him a handful. He ate it squatting on the floor.

qa.q: What did Vikas point at?
qa.a: He pointed up at the steel box of murmura.

qa.q: How can you tell Vikas felt hungry and determined?
qa.a: He tried the cupboard, then the fridge with both hands, and kept going until he found something to point at.

qa.q: What small step could Ganga try next time?
qa.a: She could keep a small snack tin where he can reach it, so he learns where food is and asks less.

qa.q: How does Ganga see his search?
qa.a: Ganga sees each try showing what he can reach and what he can't, and answers once he points.

grounding: A caregiver's note describes a toddler trying the cupboard, then the fridge, then pointing at the counter to get food.

passage:
Note for Ira's parents, from Rehana (lunch helper)
At lunch the older children said "roti!" and held out their plates. Ira watched them. Then she put out both her hands and said, "Oti!" A roti landed in them. Now, whenever food is being served, she holds out her hands and says "oti", even for rice. I gave her rice and said, "Rice." She said, "Oti," and smiled.

qa.q: What did Ira say when she held out her hands?
qa.a: She said, "Oti!"

qa.q: What was Ira thinking when she said "oti" even for rice?
qa.a: She seemed happy and confident that saying "oti" is what makes food appear.

qa.q: What else could Rehana do to build on this?
qa.a: Keep naming each food, as with rice, so Ira learns that different words ask for different things.

qa.q: How might the older children see Ira copying them?
qa.a: They might find it funny and sweet that she copies them.

grounding: A lunch helper's note describes a toddler copying others saying "roti" and holding out her hands, and using the word to make any food appear.

passage: At the evening meal in the house near the mandi in Hapur, everyone sat on the floor mat. Uncle Imran said, "Roti, please," and held out his hands. Yogesh's grandmother handed him one. Little Yogesh watched, then stuck out both hands. "Oti!" His grandmother laughed and tore him a small piece. After that he said "oti" for every dish, holding his hands out wide.

qa.q: Who said "Roti, please"?
qa.a: Uncle Imran said it.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when he got his first piece?
qa.a: He was excited and pleased that saying "oti" and holding out his hands worked.

qa.q: What would you advise the family to do next?
qa.a: Name each dish when giving it to him, so he learns more than one magic word.

qa.q: How does Yogesh's copying look to his grandmother?
qa.a: She finds it delightful and laughs, rewarding him with a piece.

grounding: A toddler copies an adult saying "roti" and holding out hands, then uses the word for every dish as a way to make food appear.

passage: Aaji was pounding spices in the village house near Satara when Omkar rubbed his tummy and said, "Num." She brought him warm milk. That was last month. Now Omkar rubs his tummy whenever he's hungry, even alone on the verandah with nobody there to see. His sister Nikita found him doing it at the empty doorway. "Aaji's at the well, Omu," she said. "Come, tell me."

qa.q: Where was Aaji when Nikita found Omkar?
qa.a: Aaji was at the well.

qa.q: What was Omkar thinking when he rubbed his tummy alone?
qa.a: He seemed hopeful and hungry, believing the rub itself would bring milk, even with no one watching.

qa.q: What else could help Omkar get food when Aaji is away?
qa.a: He could go and find someone, like Nikita, since the rub only works when someone sees it.

qa.q: How does Nikita see Omkar's tummy rub?
qa.a: Nikita finds it sweet and a bit sad that he's asking an empty doorway, so she offers to help.

grounding: A toddler who once got milk by rubbing his tummy now does it whenever hungry, even when no one is looking.

passage: Last month in the Toronto flat, Jamal rubbed his belly and said "num", and Grandma brought him milk. Since then he rubs it all the time. Today Grandma was out at the shops. Jamal stood alone in the kitchen, rubbing his belly and saying "num, num" to the fridge. When nothing came he went to the living room and rubbed it at the window.

qa.q: Where was Grandma today?
qa.a: Grandma was out at the shops.

qa.q: What was Jamal feeling when nothing came?
qa.a: He was probably puzzled and hungry, since his trusted belly rub didn't bring milk.

qa.q: What else could Jamal try when Grandma is away?
qa.a: He could look for another grown-up in the house and show them, because the rub works only when someone sees it.

qa.q: How might Grandma feel when she comes home and hears about it?
qa.a: Grandma would likely be touched and amused that he tries her trick even without her.

grounding: A toddler repeats a belly rub that once brought milk from his grandmother, even when nobody is watching.
